target.title: Add 1Password SecretRef plugin
target.body:
Related: #89255

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw has a bundled, policy-controlled 1Password broker, but operators could
not use the same plugin as a managed SecretRef provider. They had to maintain
manual exec-provider wiring to keep model and registered config credentials out
of `openclaw.json`.

## Why This Change Was Made

This extends the existing bundled `onepassword` plugin with its own managed
SecretRef integration. It keeps the two opt-in surfaces distinct: the Gateway
resolves only configured SecretRef targets, while the existing agent tool stays
curated, policy-controlled, and audited. It does not add arbitrary vault access
or make the official 1Password MCP server a plugin backend.

## User Impact

Operators can enable `onepassword` for SecretRefs without configuring the
broker's `vault`/`items` registry, save a scoped service-account token in the
plugin credentials file, generate a plan with `openclaw onepassword secretref
setup`, and apply OpenClaw SecretRefs without storing plaintext provider keys in
configuration.

## What You Can Wire

`openclaw onepassword secretref setup` does not create or upload a 1Password
secret. It records a SecretRef to an existing 1Password field, which OpenClaw
resolves only when the configured credential is needed.

The direct setup flags cover model-provider API keys:

- `--openai-id`
- `--anthropic-id`
- `--openrouter-id`
- `--provider-key <provider=id>` for any `models.providers.<provider>.apiKey`

Examples:

```bash
# Wire an existing 1Password field as OpenAI's API key.
openclaw onepassword secretref setup \
  --openai-id op://Automation/OpenAI/credential \
  --plan-out ./openclaw-1password-secrets-plan.json

# Wire a field to the Gateway token, or to any supported credential target.
openclaw onepassword secretref setup \
  --target gateway.auth.token=op://Automation/Gateway/token \
  --plan-out ./openclaw-1password-secrets-plan.json

# Wire a custom model provider API key.
openclaw onepassword secretref setup \
  --provider-key my-provider=op://Automation/MyProvider/apiKey \
  --plan-out ./openclaw-1password-secrets-plan.json

# Inspect, then apply and audit the generated plan.
openclaw onepassword secretref status --json
openclaw secrets apply --from ./openclaw-1password-secrets-plan.json --dry-run --allow-exec
openclaw secrets apply --from ./openclaw-1password-secrets-plan.json --allow-exec
openclaw secrets audit --check --allow-exec
```

`--target <config-path=id>` supports every registered OpenClaw SecretRef
credential target. This includes Gateway authentication tokens/passwords,
channel credentials, model-provider headers and request/TLS credentials,
web-search and skill API keys, supported plugin credentials, and per-agent
auth-profile API keys/tokens. The canonical generated matrix is
[`docs/reference/secretref-credential-surface.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/reference/secretref-credential-surface).

It does not permit arbitrary configuration paths, arbitrary agent vault reads,
or secret creation/rotation. The existing broker surface remains the separate,
curated agent-read path for operator-registered items.

The Gateway host must provide the official `op` CLI. Before either plugin
surface passes the service-account token to it, the plugin resolves its real
path and rejects executable or parent paths writable by another local account;
Windows ACL verification must also succeed. Desktop-app integration is disabled
for unattended reads.

The resolver accepts native `op://<vault>/<item>/<field>` and sectioned
references, plus explicit-vault shorthand. References with characters outside
the shared exec-ID grammar use a plugin-local opaque ID. Requests are bounded to
16 IDs, four concurrent `op read` calls, seven seconds per read, and a 40-second
whole-provider timeout.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/onepassword`
  - 8 extension files / 90 tests passed
- `node scripts/bundled-plugin-assets.mjs --phase copy`
- `node scripts/runtime-postbuild.mjs`
  - verified the packaged runtime copies the resolver, opaque-ID helper, and
    executable-trust helper under `dist/extensions/onepassword/`
- `git diff --check`
- fresh `autoreview --mode uncommitted`: clean
- [Inspectable redacted terminal proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/102293#issuecomment-5011541577) at the current head
- Real service-account proof using an isolated OpenClaw state and a real
  1Password concealed field:
  - selected the reference through service-account metadata only; the secret
    value was never printed, persisted, or sent to a model
  - the resolver returned one value with zero errors while
    `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN` was absent from the Gateway environment and
    read only from the plugin credential file
  - `openclaw secrets apply --from <plan> --dry-run --allow-exec` passed
  - `openclaw secrets apply --from <plan> --allow-exec` updated the isolated
    config, and `openclaw secrets audit --check --allow-exec` was clean
    (`plaintext=0`, `unresolved=0`, `shadowed=0`, `legacy=0`)
  - an isolated loopback Gateway started with that real SecretRef as
    `gateway.auth.token` and reached `[gateway] ready`; it was then stopped

The broad extension type gate was attempted after rebasing but is blocked by
existing errors in `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts`; none are in this PR.

## Review Focus

- SecretRef provider manifest and the `onepassword` ownership boundary.
- Service-account token isolation and safe `op` executable validation.
- Compatibility of generated plans and manual SecretRef references.
- The bounded resolver contract and current packaging assets.
